title: How Debt Collectors Are Transforming the Business of State Courts
pub: The Pew Charitable Trusts — Civil Legal System Modernization
author: The Pew Charitable Trusts

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not directly assess legal AI’s task-level capabilities, verification demands or work redesign. Its treatment of online dispute resolution as useful but not a panacea, requiring safeguards and evaluation, is broadly compatible with selective deployment but insufficient to establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: Since early 2019, chief justices of the supreme courts in Hawaii, Iowa, Texas, and Utah have highlighted ODR as a key priority in their State of the Judiciary addresses.107  Some jurisdictions—such as West Valley City, Utah, and Franklin County, Ohio—have begun using ODR for small debt claims in part to reduce the time that cases take to resolve.108 However, moving debt collection cases online is not a panacea.

st.t: Online disputes: Faster processing may not improve justice
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition: ODR can improve participation and court administration, but faster or remote processing does not itself establish fairer substantive outcomes. It explicitly treats reduced resolution time as an implementation aim, warns that online migration is not a cure-all, identifies risks of consumers unknowingly surrendering rights or defenses, and calls for evaluation rather than claiming demonstrated justice gains.

kp.k: Civil filings declined despite widespread unmet legal needs
kp.d: Pew reports that civil caseloads dropped more than 18 percent from 2009 to 2017, while its household survey found that more than half of U.S. households experienced a potentially court-resolvable legal issue in 2018. The report does not identify the causes of declining filings. Its subject is civil justice modernization and debt litigation, rather than AI.
qs: Civil caseloads dropped more than 18 percent from 2009 to 2017.
A recent Pew survey found that in 2018, more than half of U.S. households had a legal issue that could have been resolved in court, and that 1 in 4 households had two or more such issues.

kp.k: Debt collection became the largest civil case category
kp.d: Pew estimates that debt collection lawsuits increased from fewer than 1.7 million in 1993 to about 4 million in 2013, growing from approximately one-ninth to one-quarter of state civil cases. These estimates exclude debt claims classified as small claims and therefore likely undercount them. More recent evidence is geographically limited: Texas filings more than doubled from 2014 to 2018, but nationwide longitudinal data were unavailable.
qs: From 1993 to 2013, the number of debt cases rose from fewer than 1.7 million to about 4 million.
Both 1993 and 2013 figures are underestimated, as a significant percentage of small claims are also debt collection cases but are not counted in the contract caseloads.
The state’s small claims courts—known as justice courts—alone experienced a 140 percent increase in debt cases over that five-year period.

kp.d: The report identifies rising household debt and the emergence of debt buyers as parallel trends that may help explain increased debt litigation, rather than establishing a causal relationship. The face value of purchased debts rose from $6 billion to $98 billion between 1993 and 2013. Litigation was concentrated among a few repeat plaintiffs in some jurisdictions: nine debt buyers represented 43 percent of Massachusetts civil and small claims caseloads in 2015, and six accounted for 25 percent of Oregon civil cases from 2012 to 2016.
qs: Debt buyers are key figures in many debt collection lawsuits and may have played a significant role in the rise of civil debt cases.
During the same 20-year time frame that debt claims increased, 1993 to 2013, the total dollar value of debts purchased by debt buyers grew from $6 billion to $98 billion.

kp.k: Representation asymmetry challenges adversarial court procedures
kp.d: Pew argues that courts continue to rely on opposing parties to present facts and legal arguments despite most debt defendants lacking counsel. Studies published from 2010 through 2019 show representation in less than 10 percent of consumer debt claims, compared with nearly all plaintiffs. Jurisdictional studies associate representation with better outcomes; a Utah study covering over 165,000 cases disposed from 2015 to 2017 reported that 53 percent of represented defendants won, compared with 19 percent without representation. These comparisons are not presented as randomized causal estimates.
qs: Although civil court dockets have changed, the rules they operate on have largely stayed the same.
Consumers, however, typically have legal representation in less than 10 percent of debt claims.
However, analyses from jurisdictions across the country indicate that when consumers are represented by attorneys, they are more likely to secure a settlement or win the case outright.

kp.k: Default judgments often bypass substantive contestation
kp.d: Studies cited by Pew found default judgments in more than 70 percent of debt cases in the examined jurisdictions, not a comprehensive national sample. Defaults follow defendants' nonparticipation rather than adversarial examination of debt validity. Pew identifies practical barriers, unfamiliar debt buyers and deficient notification as possible explanations, while explicitly acknowledging limited evidence about their relative importance. Enforcement actions in California, Illinois and New York also concerned fraudulent service.
qs: Multiple studies have shown that more than 70 percent of debt cases end in default judgments:

Although the evidence on why people do not respond to the suits is scant, the available information suggests that three factors drive many of these instances: practical realities of consumers’ lives, unfamiliar plaintiffs, or a lack of notification about the suit.
As a result, debt collectors sometimes win cases that feature inaccurate information or are filed after the legal right to sue has expired.

kp.k: Judgments can intensify financial hardship and inequality
kp.d: Pew describes interest, court costs, attorney fees, garnishment and property liens as consequences that can deepen financial distress. A Maryland study found average principal of $2,811 with another $512 in costs, fees and interest. The report distinguishes prohibited imprisonment for inability to pay from relatively rare civil incarceration for noncompliance with post-judgment court requirements. It also cites research finding disproportionate effects in African American and Hispanic communities, including nearly twice the default judgment rate in mostly black versus mostly white neighborhoods after accounting for income in a five-year study of St. Louis, Chicago and Newark.
qs: Debt collection lawsuits that end in default judgment can have lasting consequences for consumers’ economic stability.
Such incarceration is relatively rare, but when it does occur, it can cause significant harm to consumers, most notably loss of wages and disruption in employment.
Research indicates that debt collections and related lawsuits disproportionately affect African American and Hispanic communities.

kp.k: Fragmented court data constrain conclusions and reform evaluation
kp.d: Pew combined approximately 70 applicable studies, expert interviews and state court statistical reports. Only 12 states publicly reported debt claims data for at least one court tier in 2018; only New Mexico and Texas reported relevant disposition data for at least one court type. Texas alone reported debt claim dispositions across all courts and dollar amounts. The underlying NCSC national study examined more than 925,000 cases in 152 courts across 10 urban counties, approximately 5 percent of national state civil caseloads. Differences in court coverage, classifications and reporting periods limit comparisons.
qs: Court systems have difficulty producing statewide reports in part because they are decentralized and fragmented and generally collect data only for their own administrative purposes.

Without better data than are currently available, however, states and researchers cannot effectively evaluate whether debt claims are increasing, what might be driving that growth, and what the implications are for consumers.

kp.k: Reforms shift proof obligations toward plaintiffs and courts
kp.d: From 2009 to 2019, 12 states changed policy through legislation or court rules to strengthen notice, documentation and protections against time-barred claims. Examples include Massachusetts address checks, New York City court-mailed notices that prevent default when returned undeliverable, and requirements to document debt ownership and amounts. Pew presents these as promising early reforms with insufficient evidence of effectiveness. The report separately identifies the CFPB's May 2019 time-barred-debt provision as a proposal, not an enacted rule.
qs: These states require that plaintiffs provide documentation as a matter of course rather than expecting defendants to ask plaintiffs to prove their cases.
The court will not enter a default judgment if the Postal Service returns the notice as undeliverable.
These efforts represent promising first steps, but further research is needed to examine their effectiveness in improving court access.

kp.k: Clear procedural information can increase consumer participation
kp.d: Pew reports that a Harvard Access to Justice Lab randomized controlled trial with Boston Municipal Court found that mailed information doubled debt defendants' participation relative to receiving no mailed information. Court initiatives include plain-language forms, multilingual information, self-help packets and alternative formats. The report emphasizes that making information available is insufficient unless it is useful and understandable to users.
qs: For example, Harvard Law School’s Access to Justice Lab conducted a randomized control trial in partnership with the Boston Municipal Court and found that debt claim defendants who received mailings from the court participated in their lawsuits at twice the rate of people who received no information by mail.
One critical consideration for courts is whether the information they provide is not merely available but in fact helpful to users.

kp.k: Online court tools offer benefits with unresolved risks
kp.d: The report discusses self-help portals, automated interviews, form completion and online dispute resolution, without identifying them as AI systems. Portals offer procedural assistance and referrals; ODR permits remote dispute handling and may help manage caseloads. West Valley City, Utah, and Franklin County, Ohio, had begun using ODR for small debt claims partly to shorten resolution times. Pew treats benefits as promising rather than established and reports Lisa Stifler's warning that consumers could unknowingly waive rights or defenses. Its recommendations combine better data, procedural reform and accessible modernization rather than technology alone.
qs: In the court context, ODR allows people to handle civil legal disputes without setting foot in a courtroom, and state and local leaders are increasingly looking to this approach to streamline people’s interactions with civil courts and help court staff better manage caseloads.
However, moving debt collection cases online is not a panacea.
ODR has the potential to offer avenues to consumers to respond to lawsuits against them, but there are concerns about consumers unknowingly waiving rights or legal claims or defenses.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The report makes no explicit claims about AI. Its related claims concern digital court services, automated self-help tools, and online dispute resolution (ODR), which it does not identify as AI.
pts.d: Pew argues that technology holds promise for improving legal information and consumer outreach. It describes online portals whose automated interviews help litigants identify legal issues and complete court forms. ODR enables participation without attending a courtroom; court leaders are looking to it to simplify interactions and help staff manage caseloads. These are descriptions of capabilities and anticipated benefits, not findings that AI replaces lawyers or transforms legal markets. Interviewed consumer advocate Lisa Stifler separately warns that ODR could lead consumers to unknowingly waive rights or defenses.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Pew supports its technology discussion with cited research, implementation examples, and expert interviews, while acknowledging limited effectiveness evidence.
pts.d: The report cites research on remote appearances, platform technology, and user access; identifies legal assistance portals in Illinois, Maine, Michigan, and Ohio; and describes ODR implementations in West Valley City, Utah, and Franklin County, Ohio. It supplies no AI benchmarks or quantified ODR effectiveness results. The strongest quantified intervention result in this discussion concerns procedural mailings, not technology: Pew reports that a Harvard Access to Justice Lab randomized controlled trial with the Boston Municipal Court found doubled participation among debt defendants receiving mailings. Stifler's risk warning comes from a June 2019 interview, rather than a measured incidence of rights waivers.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The May 2020 report presents modernization as early-stage, with benefits conditional on usability and consumer protections; it gives no AI adoption forecast.
pts.d: Pew describes existing portals and ODR pilots, and notes that chief justices in four states made ODR a priority beginning in early 2019. It does not specify when broader benefits will materialize. Information must be genuinely helpful and understandable, not merely available. ODR is expressly not a universal solution, particularly without recognized best practices. Pew proposes future evaluation of risks and benefits rather than claiming that these have already been established.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are self-represented debt defendants, other civil court users, and court staff—not AI vendors or law-firm staffing structures.
pts.d: Pew frames modernization as an access-to-justice response to overwhelmingly unrepresented consumers facing business plaintiffs. Digital information and remote processes are intended to improve accessibility, affordability, and participation; courts may gain better caseload management. Consumers also face potential rights-waiver risks. Pew suggests that procedural improvements could benefit users beyond debt claims but offers no quantified prediction of those wider effects.
